claims.text: High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings resist time-dependent plastic deformation.
A high density of coherent, lattice-mismatched interfaces acts as an effective barrier to dislocation motion.
The interfaces confine dislocations and thereby reduce creep.
The proposed multilayers have alternating layers with controlled lattice mismatch and high interface coherency.
Layer thickness and interface spacing will be varied during deposition to produce different interface densities.
The multilayers will be compared with a homogeneous HEA coating having the same overall composition.
Creep behavior will be tested under constant mechanical load at room temperature and elevated temperatures below diffusion-dominated regimes.
Coating behavior is governed by interface density and coherency between layers.
Coherent, lattice-mismatched interfaces obstruct dislocation glide and climb.
The interfaces promote dislocation confinement and pile-up.
Higher coherent-interface density will produce significantly lower creep rates than the homogeneous HEA or lower-interface-density baseline.
Higher coherent-interface density will produce reduced observable dislocation activity at interfaces.
Interface effects dominate for film thicknesses typically ranging from tens to hundreds of nanometers.
The proposed mechanism applies only at temperatures where diffusion is not the dominant deformation mechanism.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction may depend on interactions among layer thickness, lattice mismatch, and other microstructural factors.
